Ratio_Quiz.Case Name: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
Ratio_Quiz.Judgment Snippet (paraphrased, shown to: Parliament has wide power to amend the Constitution under Article 368, but this power is not unlimited.
Ratio_Quiz.Ratio Decidendi (correct answer): Parliament cannot use its amending power under Article 368 to damage or destroy the 'basic structure' of the Constitution.
Ratio_Quiz.Obiter Dicta (distractor): Individual judges' differing lists of what counts as 'basic structure' (federalism, secularism, judicial review, etc.) — illustrative, not an exhaustive binding list.

Ratio_Quiz.Case Name: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
Ratio_Quiz.Judgment Snippet (paraphrased, shown to: The petitioner's passport was impounded without being given a reason or a hearing.
Ratio_Quiz.Ratio Decidendi (correct answer): Any procedure that deprives a person of life or personal liberty under Article 21 must be fair, just, and reasonable — not arbitrary or oppressive.
Ratio_Quiz.Obiter Dicta (distractor): Broader discussion on how Articles 14, 19, and 21 together form one integrated scheme of fundamental rights.

Ratio_Quiz.Case Name: Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab
Ratio_Quiz.Judgment Snippet (paraphrased, shown to: The constitutionality of the death penalty under Section 302 IPC was challenged as violating Articles 14, 19, and 21.
Ratio_Quiz.Ratio Decidendi (correct answer): The death penalty should be imposed only in the 'rarest of rare' cases, where the alternative option of life imprisonment is unquestionably foreclosed.
Ratio_Quiz.Obiter Dicta (distractor): The illustrative (non-exhaustive) list of aggravating and mitigating circumstances a court may consider.

Ratio_Quiz.Case Name: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak case)
Ratio_Quiz.Judgment Snippet (paraphrased, shown to: A hazardous gas leak from a factory in Delhi caused injury to nearby residents.
Ratio_Quiz.Ratio Decidendi (correct answer): An enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity owes an absolute and non-delegable duty to the community, with no exceptions for 'Act of God' or third-party fault.
Ratio_Quiz.Obiter Dicta (distractor): Remarks on the need for a specialized environmental tribunal and stricter industrial regulation going forward.

Ratio_Quiz.Judgment Snippet (paraphrased, shown to: In the absence of any domestic law on the subject, the Court was asked to address workplace sexual harassment.
Ratio_Quiz.Ratio Decidendi (correct answer): In the absence of domestic legislation, international conventions (like CEDAW) can be read into Articles 14, 19, and 21 to fill the gap, and the Vishaka Guidelines are binding until Parliament legislates.
Ratio_Quiz.Obiter Dicta (distractor): Observations on employer best practices and the need for a complaints committee structure.

Ratio_Quiz.Case Name: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
Ratio_Quiz.Judgment Snippet (paraphrased, shown to: Section 66A of the IT Act criminalized sending 'offensive' messages online, and was challenged as vague and overbroad.
Ratio_Quiz.Ratio Decidendi (correct answer): Section 66A is unconstitutional as it is vague, overbroad, and has a chilling effect on the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a).
Ratio_Quiz.Obiter Dicta (distractor): Commentary distinguishing Section 66A from Sections 69A and 79 of the IT Act, which were upheld with safeguards.
